To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
1) Synapses are patterned in the cortex, and their molecular and functional properties are differentially tuned to specific cortical laminae.

the expression of synaptic molecules is a key determinant of the temporal selectivity of cortical networks, and this expression is patterned in a laminar-specific and regional-specific manner, and is subject to evolutionary and experience-dependent regulation.

the timescales of neocortical dynamics are differentially tuned to reflect the temporal properties of sensory inputs and that this selectivity is regulated by the regional expression of synaptic molecules.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mechanisms that underlie the formation and regulation of the temporal receptive windows of neocortical networks.
the mechanisms underlying the temporal selectivity of neocortical circuits and how this selectivity is modulated by synaptic patterning.
the role of synaptic patterning in the emergence of cortical selectivity to the temporal structure of sensory stimuli.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the timescales of the dynamics of cortical circuits are a function of their synaptic patterning.
the timescales of the dynamics of cortical circuits are determined by the synaptic composition, which is in turn shaped by genetic and environmental influences.
cortical dynamics and the processing thereof are shaped by the synaptic architecture of the network, which in turn is shaped by the molecular composition and the developmental history of the circuit.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

synaptic composition and plasticity are critical in determining cortical dynamics and that these properties can be modulated by environmental experience to tune the network to operate within specific temporal windows.

synaptic composition and plasticity, in conjunction with the underlying network dynamics, are likely to be the key determinants of the cortical processing of sensory information at different temporal scales.

cortical networks are not only able to represent the temporal structure of their sensory environment, but that the expression of molecular components of synaptic transmission, in conjunction with the anatomical structure of the cortex, can regulate the temporal receptive windows of cortical circuits and thereby the timescales of information processing.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the temporal selectivity of neocortical circuits is not an inherent property, but rather a result of the synaptic patterning of the cortical microcircuitry.
synaptic plasticity and its regulation by neuromodulators are likely to be the key factors in shaping the dynamics of cortical networks.
cortical networks can process sensory signals at multiple times scales, but that the relative importance of these scales is likely to depend on the regional composition of the cortical microcircuit.
